tagline: Mountain lakes at the Balkan crossroads
overview:
North Macedonia is a landlocked country in the heart of the Balkan Peninsula, about the size of Vermont and ringed by mountains, with Kosovo, Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece, and Albania as neighbors. Rivers cut down through the high country and gather in the Vardar, which flows south past the capital and on toward the Aegean Sea in Greece.

About 1.8 million people live here. Macedonian, a Slavic language written in Cyrillic, is the official language, and Albanian is co-official; roughly a quarter of the population is ethnic Albanian. Skopje, the capital, straddles the Vardar, where a stone Ottoman bridge links the old bazaar to a modern center crowded with statues. North Macedonia is a parliamentary republic and joined NATO in 2020.

The country changed its name from Macedonia to North Macedonia in 2019 under an agreement with Greece, which had objected that the old name overlapped with its own northern region of Macedonia.
landAndNature: Mountains fill most of the country: Golem Korab on the Albanian border rises to 2,764 meters, and dozens of peaks pass 2,000. Between them lie fertile basins where tobacco, peppers, and grapes ripen in hot, dry summers, while winter brings snow and skiing. Lake Ohrid, shared with Albania, is one of the oldest and deepest lakes in Europe, perhaps three million years old, and holds more than 200 species found nowhere else, including the Ohrid trout. Nearby Lake Prespa drains underground through limestone into Ohrid. Mavrovo National Park protects beech and pine forest where the rare Balkan lynx survives alongside bears, wolves, and chamois, and pelicans nest in the lake reeds.
peopleAndCulture: Macedonians and Albanians make up most of the population, with Turkish, Roma, Serb, and Vlach communities as well; Orthodox churches and mosques often stand within sight of each other. Meals are long and shared: ajvar, a red pepper relish made each autumn when families roast peppers by the sackful, tavche gravche, beans baked in a clay pot, flaky burek, and yogurt. Folk music uses the zurla, a piercing reed horn, and the tapan drum, and dancers link arms in a circle dance called the oro, often in uneven rhythms such as seven beats to a bar. Soccer and handball are the leading sports, and Skopje's bazaar has traded for some 600 years.
history: This land was part of ancient Paeonia, next to the kingdom of Macedon of Philip II and Alexander the Great, whose heartland lay in what is now northern Greece. Rome and then Byzantium ruled here, and in the 800s the disciples of Saints Cyril and Methodius spread Slavic writing from Ohrid, which became a center of learning. Ottoman rule lasted about five centuries, ending with the Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913. The territory joined Yugoslavia and became one of its six republics after World War II. It declared independence in 1991, the only republic to leave Yugoslavia without war, although a brief conflict with ethnic Albanian insurgents in 2001 ended in an agreement that expanded minority rights.
funFacts: Lake Ohrid is up to 288 meters deep and so ancient that scientists describe it as a museum of living fossils.
Kokino, a Bronze Age site of carved stone seats and markers, was used to track the rising sun about 3,800 years ago.
Mother Teresa, later a Nobel Peace Prize winner, was born in Skopje to an Albanian family in 1910.
The stone bridge over the Vardar in Skopje has carried people across the river for roughly 550 years.
North Macedonia and Greece ended a naming dispute of nearly thirty years in 2019, when the country added North to its name.
